CausalChain: GEMIN5 upregulation -> Altered interaction/regulation of BRCA1 and RAD51 (and influence on KMT5C activity) -> Shift from high-fidelity DSB repair to error-prone break-induced replication -> Increased genomic instability -> Enhanced tumor metastasis and progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated GEMIN5 expression disrupts the balance of DNA repair by directly interfacing with key repair proteins, particularly BRCA1 and RAD51, as well as indirectly modulating accessory repair factors such as KMT5C. This disruption drives a pathogenic shift from accurate homologous recombination to an error-prone break-induced replication pathway, resulting in heightened genomic instability that underlies aggressive tumor behavior and metastasis. By employing advanced techniques—such as CRISPR/Cas9 knockouts, proximity labeling to map protein–protein interactions, and single-cell multi-omics to capture heterogeneity in repair pathway engagement—we aim to validate the role of GEMIN5 as a versatile regulator of DNA repair networks, and to explore its potential as a novel therapeutic target in liver cancer.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, elevated expression of GEMIN5 may contribute to poor prognosis by remodeling the DNA repair machinery through a dual regulatory mechanism. Specifically, GEMIN5 appears to modulate canonical repair regulators such as BRCA1 and RAD51, while also influencing factors like KMT5C that are known to promote homologous recombination. We hypothesize that GEMIN5 acts as a molecular scaffold that shifts the balance from high-fidelity double-strand break (DSB) repair to an error-prone break-induced replication (BIR) process, thereby escalating genomic instability and facilitating tumor metastasis. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as CRISPR-based perturbation, proximity labeling, and single-cell multi-omics, our approach aims to delineate the specific protein–protein interactions and transcriptional shifts driven by GEMIN5 in a subset of liver cancers. This integrated strategy not only refines the mechanistic understanding of GEMIN5-mediated dysregulation of DSB repair, but also positions GEMIN5 and its interacting network as potential therapeutic targets that may modulate aggressive tumor behavior.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that GEMIN5 upregulation disrupts the double-strand break repair process via direct interference with BRCA1 and RAD51, leading to genomic instability and metastasis. The revised hypothesis retains this central causal chain but expands it by integrating additional regulatory elements (notably KMT5C) and incorporating a dual mechanistic perspective: GEMIN5 not only disrupts classical repair factor interactions but also rebalances repair pathway choice toward error-prone break-induced replication. Furthermore, the new hypothesis leverages contemporary technological advances (CRISPR screening, proximity labeling, and single-cell multi-omics) to enhance experimental rigor in dissecting the GEMIN5-centered network. This revision aligns with the original causal chain—GEMIN5 upregulation -> dysregulation of DNA repair regulators -> impaired DSB repair via BIR -> increased genomic instability -> enhanced tumor metastasis and progression—while addressing identified gaps and integrating modern methodological approaches to validate the proposed mechanism.
